_readme: THE LIVE TO-DO LIST, AS DATA. This file is the source. to-do.md's ranked table is
GENERATED from it by `npm run to-do`, and the Handbook's ranking control reads it.
Edit here — an edit to that table is overwritten.
A list saved from the control comes back with `npm run to-do -- <file>`. It is
validated against the five fields first, and an item Mike settles is NOT removed
until its closure is written on to-do-done-and-parked.md — the command applies
nothing at all until then. An item gone from both pages is an item nobody knows
existed.
FORMATTING IS THE SCRIPT'S. Applying a saved list rewrites this file with two-space
JSON, so do not hand-tune the layout; it will not survive.
Every item must carry all five fields the list's own rules demand — score, why,
risk, askedBy, touches — and tests/unit/toDoItems.test.js fails the build if one
is missing. That guard is the whole reason this file exists: an item missing a
field is a note, and notes are what produced two pieces of unrequested work on
EVERY FIELD HAS A WORD CAP, and tests/unit/toDoItems.test.js fails the build past it:
name 16, why 40, risk 80, touches 80, note 120, comment 120, askedBy.detail 80. A
session with more to say than that puts it in the feature's Brief or history file
and links it. ONE FACT, ONE HOME: replace a sentence that is out of date; never append
an UPDATED paragraph beneath it. On 2026-09-03 one item's comment had grown to 1,388
words across seven sessions that way, and Mike could not read his own list.
activeOn: { machine, since } says which computer is working an item right now —
'laptop' or 'desktop', from the date given. Mike's instruction, 2026-09-03, after item
4.54 was built on both machines in the same week. Absent means nobody is on it. The
page shows it as a column, the control shows it on the row, and the control's save
carries it through. Shutdown clears or keeps it; startup reports the other machine's.
rankedByMike: false marks an item filed after orderedByMikeOn that Mike has not yet
placed. The page and the Handbook control show it. It clears itself: the control's
export does not carry the field, so his next saved list drops it.
ORDER IS MIKE'S RANKING. The array order is the order on screen. It is not
computed from the score, and it must never be re-sorted by a script or a session.
Where his order and the score disagree, his order wins and the score stays
visible so the disagreement is on the page.
KIND — 'defect' or 'feature', and it is a GATE, not a label. A defect is something
that already exists being wrong, missing, unverified or unmaintainable. A feature is a
new capability, page, screen or behaviour. tests/unit/toDoItems.test.js FAILS THE BUILD
on a feature whose askedBy.ours is true — a new thing nobody outside asked for cannot be
filed at all. A defect we found ourselves still can, because Mike never asked us to stop
reporting bugs; he asked us to stop inventing work.
SCORE — 5 security/privacy/data integrity · 4 the user is worse off · 3 helps
sell the package · 2 robustness · 1 internal only · 0 is not filed, it is
deleted with its code.
askedBy.ours = true means NOBODY OUTSIDE ASKED. It is not a defect to record it;
it is a defect to hide it. An item that cannot name Mike or a named outsider has
to justify itself.

items.name: First-year depreciation cannot differ from later years, or between two vehicles
items.why: The engine applies one rate to a whole category for every month, so a new asset cannot be written down faster in its first year than the old one beside it.
items.risk: Mike's example, costed against NZ's Investment Boost (20% of a new asset's cost deducted up front, the rest depreciated as normal): an 800,000 tractor unit deducts 146,118 in year one as the engine models it, against 276,895 with the boost. That is 36,617 of tax in year one and 130,776 of asset value carried into year two. A forecast a lender reads would be wrong, and balance perfectly.

askedBy.detail: 2026-09-08 - 'it might make a difference if it is a large purchase - like an $800,000 truck/tractor unit in terms of tax to pay and working capital balance year 2 - perhaps worth making as another task?' Raised by him while ruling question 4 of the 4.65 drawing.

items.touches: server/report/threeWayForecastModel.js assetSchedule, which applies one depreciationRate per category across twelve months, and the six-category shape in ASSET_SPECS. A per-asset or first-year rate changes the engine's asset model, so the golden set and every forecast test move with it. No screen exists to enter such a rate.
items.note: NOT A BIGGER VERSION OF 4.65 - a different asset model. assetSchedule applies one rate to a whole pool every month; a first-year rule needs assets carrying a rate or deduction that changes at a date. MYOB's per-asset rates do NOT deliver it - one standing rate per asset, no first-year concept, and QuickBooks gives no rate at all. SOURCE STILL NEEDED: Investment Boost is cited from an AI session's own knowledge, NOT from the two IRD files Mike supplied - IR265 (October 2023) and IR260 (April 2024) both predate it - both read in full 2026-09-08, zero mentions. Only THAT rule lacks a source. UK and Australia have their own regimes, unchecked here.
items.comment: 2026-09-08 - raised and filed by Mike while ruling question 4 of the asset-schedule drawing, and costed on his own example. Same day: a session wrongly reported that NZ had abolished first-year acceleration, reading the 2010 end of the 20% LOADING as the end of all such rules. Mike corrected it. The two are different mechanisms - the loading inflated a rate, Investment Boost deducts a slice of cost.

items.name: Tax rules per country - a firm manager uploads the source, the AI proposes, they approve
items.why: Depreciation rates and first-year rules differ by country and nothing in the app holds them. The shipped defaults are a guess: Vehicles is 20% where NZ IRD gives 50% diminishing value for a passenger vehicle.
items.risk: An advisor who leaves a default produces a forecast whose depreciation, tax and closing cash are all wrong, and which balances perfectly, and it reaches a lender. The counter-risk is the AI misreading a rate nobody re-checks - which is why the manager approves the extracted table before anything reads it, and why every figure carries its source document and date.

askedBy.detail: 2026-09-08 - 'is it worth having a field in the firm manager hub where tax pdfs can be loaded to be read by the AI so it can be accurate per country?' Filed on his yes, after he overturned the recommendation against it: the uploader is an accountant who should be encouraged to check their sources.

items.touches: A new Firm Manager Hub tab and its upload route, the untrusted-file validation procedure in the master-export-upload skill (last-known-good, version history), an OpenAI extraction route on the Restify backend, an approval gate carrying isApproved, and the six ASSET_SPECS defaults in components/ThreeWayForecastIntake.vue that it would replace.
items.note: AI PROPOSES, THE MANAGER APPROVES, AND NOTHING READS AN UNAPPROVED TABLE - CLAUDE.md already requires this for financial output (isApproved before committing). Every rate shows its source document and date. IT MUST ALSO SHOW WHAT THE AI COULD NOT FIND: on 2026-09-08 a session read IR260 and IR265 in full and still concluded NZ had no first-year regime, because Investment Boost postdates both - a gap invisible from inside the file. SIX QUESTIONS RULED 2026-09-08 on design/mockups/tax-rules-upload.html: the FIRM owns it, full cascade, an advisor LOADS and only the manager APPROVES. Both screens are drawn; the advisor's is tax-rules-advisor.html, with three questions open. Tax PDFs are public, so no PII question arises.
items.comment: 2026-09-08 - raised by Mike and filed on his instruction the same day. The recommendation was AGAINST it and he overturned it: the uploader is a firm manager who knows the topic and should be encouraged to check their sources. The concern that survived was not who uploads but who checks the extraction, which the approve-before-use gate answers.
